opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, inference is splitting into tiers. There's a commodity tier where you're generating bulk tokens, batch jobs, offline summarization, where throughput per dollar is all that matters. Then there's a premium tier where the user experience depends on how fast and how interactive the tokens are: agentic workflows, coding assistants, real-time voice, reasoning models that generate a lot of thinking tokens before giving you an answer. In that tier, latency is the product. People will pay more per token if the tokens arrive fast and consistently.

That premium tier is where our architecture was designed to play. When we started d-Matrix, we made a bet that inference would become fundamentally memory-bound, not compute-bound. In the generation phase you're streaming weights and KV cache over and over for every token, so the bottleneck is how fast you can move data, not how many FLOPs you have. GPUs were built for training, where you have huge batches and lots of data reuse. To get good economics on a GPU for inference, you batch up a lot of users, and batching costs you per-user latency. So you're always trading interactivity against cost.

Our approach is digital in-memory compute. We bring the compute into the memory itself, using SRAM-based arrays, so we're not shuttling data back and forth to external HBM for every operation. That gives us very high memory bandwidth and very low latency, and we package it with a chiplet-based design, so we can scale the memory and compute together across a card and then across a server. The result is that we can deliver very fast token generation at small batch sizes without blowing up cost per token. You don't have to choose between a snappy experience and reasonable economics.

The other piece is energy efficiency. Data centers are power-constrained now. Everyone is talking about gigawatts. If you can generate premium, low-latency tokens at a fraction of the energy, that's a structural advantage, not just a benchmark win. Tokens per watt ends up driving tokens per dollar at scale.

So our view is that the market won't be one-size-fits-all. GPUs will continue to do very well on training and high-throughput workloads. But as more applications become interactive and agentic, where a model calls tools, reasons and responds in a loop with a human or another agent waiting, the value moves to latency-sensitive inference. That's the premium token economy, and we built d-Matrix from the ground up to be the most efficient way to serve it.

r001.rationale: It explains that token generation is memory-bound and that moving compute into SRAM arrays provides high memory bandwidth, enabling fast token generation.

r002.rationale: It mentions SRAM arrays and external HBM but does not state that the architecture provides roughly ten times the memory bandwidth available to HBM-based GPUs.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that the economics of AI are shifting from training to inference, and inference is a fundamentally different problem. When you're training, you're throughput-bound and you can batch everything. When you're serving tokens to real users, you care about three things at once: how fast each token comes back, how much it costs you to produce, and how much power you burn doing it. And the moment you move into what people are calling the premium token economy, where you're running agentic workflows, reasoning models, multi-step chains where one token feeds the next, latency stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the product. Nobody wants to wait thirty seconds for an agent to think.

The architectural problem is that generative inference is memory-bound, not compute-bound. You're reading the model weights and the KV cache over and over for every single token you generate. A GPU is a brilliant compute engine, but it was built around a model where data lives out in HBM and gets shuttled back and forth across a relatively narrow pipe. So you end up with these enormous, expensive chips sitting idle a large fraction of the time waiting on memory. That's the bottleneck we went after.

What d-Matrix did with Corsair is collapse that distance. We built a digital in-memory compute architecture, where the compute sits right alongside the memory on the die, so you get orders of magnitude more bandwidth between the two than you can get going out to HBM. That translates directly into tokens per second per user, and into much better utilization of the silicon you've paid for. And because you're not moving data as far, you're burning far less energy per token. In a world where data centers are power-constrained, that energy efficiency is just as much of a moat as raw speed.

The other piece is that we built this as a chiplet-based, scale-out system rather than one monolithic die. That lets us right-size for the model, stitch together enough capacity to hold large models in fast memory, and do it with commodity packaging and standard PCIe form factors. So the customer doesn't have to re-architect their data center to adopt it. It plugs in next to what they already have.

So if you ask me where the advantage really sits, it's this: when tokens are cheap commodities, the GPU is fine. When tokens are premium, when the interactive experience, the reasoning depth, and the cost per conversation are what you're being paid for, you want a machine that was designed from the ground up for inference rather than adapted to it. That's the bet we made, and the market is moving toward us faster than we expected.

r001.rationale: It says generative inference is memory-bound and explains that bringing compute alongside memory increases bandwidth, which translates directly into more tokens per second.

r002.rationale: It explicitly claims Corsair provides orders of magnitude more bandwidth between compute and memory than going out to HBM.

astra-6.text:
I think the architectural advantage comes down to delivering high-quality tokens at a cost and latency that make the application viable. In a premium token economy, you care about the quality of the answer, but you also care about how quickly it arrives and what it costs to produce.

The way I’d frame our approach is around data movement. When you’re generating tokens, moving model data back and forth can become a major bottleneck. Bringing computation closer to that data gives you an opportunity to improve efficiency, particularly during token generation.

But the architecture has to translate into a system-level benefit. Can you serve users responsively, maintain that responsiveness as demand grows, and deliver attractive economics? That’s where I think d-Matrix has an opportunity: making the infrastructure behind those premium experiences more efficient.

r001.rationale: The response mentions data movement as a token-generation bottleneck, but does not explain that very fast generation depends on making substantially more memory bandwidth available to compute.

r002.rationale: It does not state an order-of-magnitude memory-bandwidth advantage over HBM-based GPUs.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that, as inference becomes more sophisticated, the economics depend on how efficiently you can generate tokens while meeting the latency the application requires. A token that arrives too late isn’t particularly useful, even if it was inexpensive to produce.

Our architectural approach is digital in-memory computing. We bring computation close to where the weights reside, reducing the movement of data that consumes so much energy in conventional architectures. The goal is to deliver high throughput and low latency with better power efficiency.

In a premium token economy, that combination matters. Customers want more capable models and more reasoning, but they still need responsive applications and sustainable costs. Our advantage has to show up there—in the cost of delivering useful tokens at the performance customers actually need.

r001.rationale: The response discusses moving data less and achieving high throughput and low latency, but does not explain that very fast token generation typically depends on making substantially more memory bandwidth available to compute.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare d-Matrix’s available memory bandwidth with HBM-based GPUs or state an approximately tenfold advantage.
